/THURSDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Issued at 211 AM MST Mon Nov 9 2026

GEFS and EC ensemble guidance are consistent with northwesterly flow 
overhead at 500-mb Thursday morning as a strong 70-90 kt jet streak 
pushes troughing deep into the Eastern United States, and ridging 
begins to move in overhead. Post-frontal northerly winds are 
forecast to be in place during the morning and afternoon hours 
Thursday, aided by a surface high centered in Southern Canada. High 
temperatures are currently forecast in the mid 50s to mid 60s, with 
the coolest temperatures along and east of a line from McCook, NE to 
Gove City, KS where northerly winds will have the greatest impact. 
It should be noted that NBM guidance shows a large amount of 
uncertainty in high temperatures along and east of Kansas Highway 
27, where the difference in 75th and 25th percentile forecast highs 
are between 10 and 15 degrees. This zone has an 80% chance or 
greater for wind gusts less than 15 MPH, and a 40-60% chance of less 
than 10 MPH. When paired with a lack of cloud cover due to 
subsidence across the region, highs in the 60s may be experienced 
across the east as well. No hazards are expected Thursday, though 
some areas may drop to or just below freezing overnight. 

Ensembles support ridging overhead at least on Friday and Saturday, 
as two troughs come into the Western United States. Weak southerly 
surface flow is likely through most of this period. Highs are 
forecast similar to Thursday both days, with slightly higher 
temperatures in the east on Saturday. A large spread in the NBM high 
temperatures continues to exist, with 75th and 25th percentile 
forecasts differing by up to 20 F on Friday. However, considering 
that ridging is in place alongside weak southerly flow, temperatures 
in the 60s or higher are currently favored both Friday and Saturday, 
with some areas potentially able to reach into the 70s depending on 
how much solar heating takes place. 

Sunday is where the forecast begins to become a little more 
uncertain, specifically regarding the two troughs coming in from the 
Western United States. One is a weaker shortwave ejection from the 
Desert Southwest, and another is a deeper longwave from the Pacific 
Northwest. The southern system gets relatively muted in the 
ensembles, while deterministics have shown variability in the 
timing, intensity, and track of the system. Additionally, the most 
recent EC ensemble run shows the northern system ejecting in front 
of the southern system. This could be supported by the fact that all 
ensembles show large amounts of variability on the trailing edge of 
the southern system, which would indicate a potentially slower 
progression. What is a bit more certain is that cooler, wetter 
conditions are expected as these systems come through. NBM 24 hr 
precipitation guidance shows around a 25% chance across the area 
that greater than 0.1 inches of rain occurs between Monday night and 
Tuesday night, which could be experienced earlier if one of these 
systems progresses into the area Sunday or early Monday. 
Additionally, NBM guidance suggests that highs in the 40s and 
50s would be most likely with these systems. However, if these 
systems do progress slower, conditions similar to Thursday 
through Saturday will continue. When looking at precipitation 
guidance from the LREF, only about 15% of the members show 
precipitation occurring Sunday, alongside 75% showing 
temperatures above 60. This would suggest a favored slower 
progression where warmer and drier conditions continue to 
prevail through the weekend. Around 40% of the members show 
precipitation Monday, and over 50% Tuesday, suggesting that 
these systems are most likely to move in around the beginning of
next week.
